speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The PRGT is the IMF's concessional lending vehicle, which provides lending facilities tailored to the diverse needs of low-income countries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To fund the PRGT, IMF members agreed in 2012 to contribute at least 90% of distributed profits from the sales of gold holdings at the IMF.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a highly open economy and international financial centre, Singapore has a strong stake in preserving a healthy global economic environment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This includes doing our part in the IMF's efforts to assist low-income countries.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The PRGT will help support developing countries in Asia, such as Cambodia, Lao PDR, Myanmar and Vietnam, whom we share growing economic ties with.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Any future grant to the IMF will also require Parliament's approval.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: MAS currently has powers to provide loans and interest-free deposits to the IMF under the MAS Act, but not grants.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the Bill will empower MAS to make grants to the IMF, but only with Parliament's approval.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments will also consolidate MAS' existing powers to provide financial assistance to the IMF, including loans and interest-free deposits, into this single Act.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The second key provision is about setting out strong safeguards when providing financial assistance to the IMF.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Bill will add the following safeguards that apply when MAS provides any loans, grants or other financial assistance to the IMF.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, any financial assistance can only be provided pursuant to a specific request from the IMF.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition, MAS will provide financial assistance only as part of collective action among IMF members.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, in the interest of transparency, the Minister-in-charge of MAS must publish in the Gazette a statement containing key information about the financial assistance.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This statement will contain a description of the nature and terms of the agreement to lend, give grants or other financial assistance, and the maximum amount that MAS has agreed to lend or give to the IMF.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While MAS has in the past issued media statements and provided answers in Parliament on such assistance, such as in the case of MAS' contingent loan to the IMF in 2012, a Gazette notice, as required in this Bill, will provide further transparency.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is because grants are treated as expenses.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is unlike loans to IMF which are to be repaid at maturity and are recorded as assets in MAS' balance sheet.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Loans to the IMF remain part of Singapore's Official Foreign Reserves, which are managed by MAS as the central bank.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me touch on some of the provisions for early repayment.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, agreements to provide loans to the IMF include a safeguard that obliges the IMF to immediately repay the loan in the event that Singapore has a balance of payments need.

speaker: The Minister for National Development (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The introduction of the Bretton Woods Agreements (Amendment) Bill will enable Singapore to support the IMF initiative to help low-income countries in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The PRGT was set up primarily to lend to low-income countries who may be severely impacted by catastrophes, natural disasters, epidemics or global financial crises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The amendments also instituted additional safeguards, such as requiring Parliament's approval for the provision of the grants and that the Minister-in-charge of MAS must also publish in the Gazette a statement containing details of the financial agreement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I support the amendment to empower MAS, as well as the safeguards put in place over MAS' exercise of powers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From a humanitarian standpoint, I would also agree with the Government's position that we need to do our part and contribute our humble share to help poorer countries impacted by various calamities from time to time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also in our interest to see greater international cooperation in dealing with the various global challenges that we face and for the spirit of Bretton Woods to come to bear and continue.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, we hope to live in a global village where the community of nations make efforts to help one another in need and each doing our part to alleviate poverty.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Mdm Speaker, I do have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand from the Minister's speech that the additional funds for the PRGT initiative is paid for from the profits arising from the IMF's sales of part of its gold holdings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is against the backdrop of the growing trend of Western countries under political pressure to reduce their commitment to foreign aid.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the PRGT be able to self-sustain its concessionary lending capacity over the long term with this latest contribution?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is the rationale and why would we not require more governments to participate before we assist, given that IMF is a multilateral participatory organisation?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this case, I understand that PRGT has already obtained support of more than 80% of the member countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a highly open economy and international financial centre, it would also serve us well to support IMF's multilateral efforts to improve the livelihood of poorer countries, develop sustainable economic growth and preserve global financial stability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have seen how many bigger countries had faced economic crises because of their lack of prudence in safeguarding their reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This does not include such earthquakes in the financial market as the collapse of the subprime market in the US, the Eurozone debt crisis, the recent sharp decline in oil prices and other commodities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Governments need to carefully scrutinise their spending and to be honest when making hard decisions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The leaders must take the honourable step to be prepared to explain to the people on any difficult decisions rather than take the road of least resistance to win popularity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, the IMF is called into play to help support or rescue governments for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Across the globe, Angola is the latest to seek a bailout from the IMF that could be worth more than US$1.5 billion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This oil-producing OPEC member is seeking international help to cope with the fallout from low crude prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Others, like Greece, are still struggling and tapping on IMF bailout funds.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore, as a small nation, can take pride in being able to contribute to the IMF.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We even hosted the 61st annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank board of governors in 2006.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, we are also the home for the IMF-Singapore Training Institute, serving as the regional training centre for the Asia-Pacific region on macroeconomic and financial management.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the case of grants, additional safeguards were set out with the need for Parliament's approval.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is, powers to give grants to the IMF are subject to Parliament's approval, given the nature of grants as an expense and not an asset.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, while I support the amendment Bill, I would like to ask the Minister a few questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I feel we should put a limit based on a percentage of our current GDP or of our reserves, with a cap on a maximum, whichever is lower.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is on top of what is in subsection 2(d) which has already stated that Parliament will, by resolution, fix the maximum amount of grants to be given by MAS.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because any loan or grant to the IMF under any agreement will be paid out of MAS' reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, under subsection 2(c)(ii), the maximum amount that MAS agrees to lend or to give by way of grants or other financial assistance, will the methodology behind the calculation to derive that maximum amount be made public?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, for the loan component in section 6(A) subsection (4), can the Minister also share with the House, if, for some reason, Singapore faces a balance of payment crisis – as the Minister have mentioned earlier – and we are in need of the fund, what is the minimum timeframe required to notify them of our need for earlier repayments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, for accountability and transparency, under subsection 2(c), in conjunction with the Minister's published Gazette, will MAS publish the statement on the maximum amount of financial assistance in the local media on the key information about the agreement to extend financial assistance so that the public can scrutinise it, and to publish it before Parliament debates the issue?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think what is important is for all governments to work together to find a way to strengthen and maintain global financial stability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our participation via IMF would, in some ways, be contributing to bringing stability to the recipient country or countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, a country which is trying to rebuild its economy would find its efforts scuppered by crisis in another country.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, we have been enjoying financial stability though we are occasionally tested by outside events.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Stability also means we need to continually ensure that our citizens are able to take some of the jabs without suffering a knock-out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, our main defensive block is our reserves.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we must ensure we have sufficient safeguards with regard to any matter that affects our official or MAS' reserves, no matter how small.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our second defensive block is our sound fiscal position and prudent yet progressively smart financial regulatory policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our policies have shored up our banks and financial system and we need to continually keep up with the changes in the market environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our de facto central bank, MAS, has done well to mitigate any sharp rise in market volatility and has ensured the appropriate monetary conditions for the economy to grow sustainably.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope that as we participate to ensure global financial stability, we continue to ensure our own defensive blocks are not marginally eroded.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Who would have thought that oil prices, for example, could spiral down from above US$100 to just a quarter of its previous price?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many governments are caught in this sinkhole and would be at wits end how to re-write the budgets for the projects that are already launched and are work-in-progress.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The recent Brexit has added more uncertainties and chaos to the world economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, Singapore is in a happy position for it is able to participate and contribute to the IMF financial assistance scheme to help bail out others who are less fortunate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We would have read in the media of countries where the people see their savings eroded almost overnight.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We would have read of people who desperately rushed to queue for hours outside the banks and at ATMs to withdraw whatever was left in their account.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, we would have read of how families suffered because of job losses due to the collapse in their country's economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The bailout terms would require the borrowing governments to make painful cuts in expenditures, resulting in job losses.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, those whose jobs were affected would take to the streets and protest.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are all very frightening scenarios which happened in other countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Thankfully, we do not see this in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we are in a more fortunate situation where we are among the members of the IMF who are able to make contributions to offer loans and grants to others.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We had benefited from the World Bank funding our projects in the past.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Going forward, what is important for us now is to examine how do we keep a lookout for any headwinds that may be heading towards us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or should this information sharing be published in the main local media so that everyone knows under what terms the loans or assistance are given?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This way, it would thwart any attempt for mischievous rumour-mongering to make its way around the new media platforms.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the process before the proposal is tabled before Parliament?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And how much lead time will Members of Parliament have to study the proposal before it is tabled for the House to approve?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a country, we have benefited from our membership in the institutions, especially in our early years as a developing nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned by the hon Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Page: 56 Singapore received loans from the World Bank – about 14 loans between 1963 and 1975 – to develop our sewage, water, power and telecommunications infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Now, it is right for us to do our part to support the IMF in its effort to provide assistance to the development of low-income member countries (LICs), particularly under the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We live in an increasingly complex world, interconnected and interdependent, where no one country is really immune from developments in another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I quote the President of the World Bank Group, Mr Jim Yong Kim, in a speech he delivered on 5 April 2016: "It has never been so painfully clear that the world is deeply interconnected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Major issues that evolve in a developing country now swiftly move to affect developed countries – and vice versa – more than ever before.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Climate change, pandemics, refugees, terrorism and economic downturns all move seamlessly around the world." The above-mentioned impact applies all the more to an open economy like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the amendments proposed in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While the intentions and motivations are commendable, given that this involves matters of our country's finances, I would like to highlight four areas of concern in respect of the applicable safeguards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the proposed new section 6A of the Bill requires that the MAS be satisfied that at least one other government has provided or intends to provide financial assistance in response to a similar request from the IMF to provide financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Liang feels that this is setting the bar too low.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, in the explanatory brief issued by MAS on 9 May 2016, MAS said that it would only agree to a request for financial assistance where there is a collective and broad-based response among IMF members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Loans are treated as monetary assets and are recorded as such in MAS' books.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this reason, the proposed new section 6A(d) specifically requires Parliamentary approval on the quantum of the grant before a grant may be given.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree that the Parliamentary safeguard is necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, we have another safeguard in the form of the Elected President.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could the Minister please clarify whether this constitutional safeguard would apply to a loan or grant given to the IMF, given that it will be paid out of MAS' reserves?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, in the context of grants, would MAS be expected to engage the President before or after Parliament is asked to provide approval?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, where loans to the IMF are concerned, have we considered the possibility that such loans may not be repaid at maturity and may eventually be written-off?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I highlight this, in particular, as the wording of the proposed section 6A of the Act contemplates that the financial Page: 57 assistance requested by the IMF may be provided directly to a recipient country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This approach of providing assistance directly to the recipient country is also contemplated in other legislatures, such as the Australian legislature.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, Singapore would be taking on the direct credit risk of the recipient country and not the credit risk of the IMF.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As such, if there is a loan default situation, what would be the treatment of the decision to write-off such loans?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it be treated as an expenditure of MAS' reserves?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would a write-off require Parliamentary and Presidential approval under the proposed Bill or the Constitution?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Fourth, I have a concern relating to the phrase "other financial assistance" in the proposed section 6A of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Section 8C of the Australian International Monetary Agreements Act is similar to our section 6A in that it allows Australia to provide assistance to another country in support of a fund programme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Australian Act is restricted in the scope of financial assistance that may be provided as it only allows the Treasurer of Australia to enter into an agreement to lend money or to enter into a currency swap.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In our proposed section 6A, the wording is wider.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Could the Minister please clarify, besides interest-free deposits which have been identified by the MAS in its explanatory brief, what other types of financial assistance are contemplated and will they likely be also drawn from MAS' reserves?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, does section 6A contemplate the giving of guarantees?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If so, does this not engage Article 144(1) of the Constitution, such that the President's concurrence is required before the guarantee may be given?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These amendments will result in more financial assistance for lower income member countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In April this year, IMF chief, Christine Lagarde, warned that time was running out to revive the global economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A few months before that, a report to G20 leaders called for strong policy Page: 58 responses at the national and multilateral levels to propel the global economy to a more prosperous path.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does not take an economist to realise that we are entering into a changing economic climate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The global economy is facing latent fissures in the form of falling oil prices and China's slowdown.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Amid these economic threats, global powers are also struggling to cope with the refugee crisis, religious extremism and political unrest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We know that the IMF – as the global crisis lender – is not optimistic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After careful observations of global trends, they have cut their global growth forecast for the fourth time this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments allowing for increased contributions to the IMF will allow it to fight fires in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Crisis prevention is an international effort, and Singapore must act, contribute and help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A strong Singaporean response in a time like this can only signal our resolve to maintain global stability, placing Singapore at the forefront and as a leader.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This act of global goodwill will also bode us well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For a trade-reliant country like ours, a stable and healthy global economy will only serve our interests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contributing to IMF's war chest and bolstering emergency funds for weaker economies, we are, ultimately, building a firewall for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In these times of uncertainty, we must do all we can to ensure the global economic climate remains favourable to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this is not just about the Singapore economy, Singapore's interest and dollars and cents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also about showing that, despite being a tiny red dot, we can be a shining example of a small country with a big impact, a small country of responsible global citizens and we can be a shining red dot.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For me, this really is about sharing and giving – the lessons we teach our children in schools and the lessons I am currently teaching my daughter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When she is playing with other children and they want to play with the toy she is playing with, I tell her to share.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let others also have a chance to play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also teaching her to give and donate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I started passing her coins to put into donation tins in shops and explain to her why she is putting the coins in the tins.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am afraid this has been a failed experiment so far.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But she does enjoy putting the coins in the tins and she now insists on putting coins in every donation tin we walk past.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I mentioned previously that she has learnt to say the word "no", but I am afraid I have not learnt to say the word "no" to her, especially when she has now learnt the words, "Daddy, please".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am sure she will eventually understand why she is putting coins in tins.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, the best way to teach is to show by example.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As parents, we need to show that we share and we give.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a Government, we need to lead by example and show that we not just teach sharing and giving in our schools but that we practise what we preach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While the Members have highlighted the continued relevance of the IMF in maintaining a stable global financial and economic environment and the importance for Singapore to do our part in the IMF's multilateral efforts to assist low-income countries, they have also raised a number of issues and I will address them in turn.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, Mr Liang asked if the grant to the IMF's PRGT will constitute an expense on our official foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not Singapore's gold or members' gold.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And when the IMF sold its gold to raise funds for the PRGT, the proceeds arising from the gold sales were distributed to members in proportion to their quota shares, provided members agreed to contribute the proceeds as grants to the PRGT.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the proceeds from the gold sales in 2012 and 2013, due to MAS, were recorded as income in the IMF's books temporarily and would be exactly offset when MAS makes the grant to PRGT.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The net effect of this is that this entire transaction – income and outflow of grants – will not affect our overall level of official foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As countries around the world face increased risks of economic and financial disruptions arising from a broad range of factors, the IMF will review its financial assistance toolkit from time to time to see how it can assist countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where new initiatives are proposed, we will consider contributing to such initiatives where relevant and as part of a multi-lateral effort.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I have said earlier, any future grant will also similarly be subject to Parliament's approval.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is on the first point about the transaction mechanism, and whether it has an impact on our official foreign reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, Mr Liang also asked whether PRGT will be self-sustaining and if we expect more requests from member countries by IMF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Self-sustainability is, indeed, one of the key considerations for the PRGT fundraising initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is an estimate that the IMF has already made to ensure that the PRGT is on a sound, sustainable financial footing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, Mr Liang and Mr Murali asked about the rationale behind section 6A(2b) of the Bill which requires that MAS be satisfied that at least one other government has provided or intends to provide financial assistance in response to the IMF request, before MAS can agree to such requests.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thus, the key phrase is "at least one other government" but, in practice, I would like to assure Members that MAS will carefully assess any IMF requests for financial assistance on a case-by-case basis and we will participate only where it is in our interest to do so and only as part of a multilateral effort.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And as Mr Liang highlighted, IMF has acted with about 80% of IMF members, which is more than 140 countries, pledging grants with the PRGT from members' shares of the IMF's gold sales proceeds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Page: 60 Next, Mr Murali also asked if Article 22B(6) and (7) of the Constitution – basically, the Constitutional safeguards on the reserves – would apply to any of the financial assistance to the IMF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, indeed, as with any such proposed transaction, including any financial assistance to the IMF, the President would be informed if MAS has to draw on past reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If Article 22B(6) of the Constitution is engaged because a grant is likely to draw on past reserves, then MAS will inform the President before going to Parliament to obtain a resolution.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in this context, I would like to reassure Members that we do not expect any financial assistance to the IMF to require funding from past reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do not expect any financial assistance to IMF to have to be funded from past reserves as MAS is most unlikely to participate in any scheme should this arise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Murali also asked about the possibility that loans with the IMF may not be repaid.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we provide a loan in support of an IMF programme for the benefit of one or more countries, we are providing the loan to the IMF and entering into an agreement with the IMF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are taking on the credit risk of the IMF rather than the direct credit risk of the countries that the IMF lends to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is similar to the low risk that is associated with the MAS' subscriptions to the capital of the IMF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The IMF, with the advantage it has from its preferred creditor status and sizeable reserves that it can use to protect its members, has always repaid its own creditors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Murali also raised the question about what forms of other financial assistance MAS would make under the Bill and whether this includes the giving of guarantees and if the Bill should specify the types of financial assistance that can be given.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We expect these to be the main forms of assistance that MAS would give to the IMF in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have not been approached to give a guarantee to the IMF nor do we expect to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think the Member highlighted Article 144 of the Constitution stating that "no guarantee or loan should be given or raised by the Government unless the President concurs".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Article 144 does not apply to loans raised or guarantees given by a person other than the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And MAS is a separate vehicle from the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As such, Article 144 of the Constitution will not be engaged.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nevertheless, I should reiterate that MAS has not had to assist the IMF in the past by giving a guarantee; we have never had to do that and we do not expect to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if a limit should be set over the total financial assistance that can be provided to the IMF and whether there should be some form of methodology to derive this total amount that is stipulated in our various agreements with the IMF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I want to emphasise that the MAS considers each IMF request for financial assistance carefully and exercises a high degree of prudence on whether or not to contribute.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It may not be so practical to set the limit, given that there will be times of crisis when we think we should do our part to contribute to IMF resourcing initiatives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, indeed, this was the case in 2012, when we provided a contingent loan to the IMF at the time of heightened global risk.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, I think I should also elaborate that, as I have said earlier in my opening speech, it is in Singapore's interest to do our part to contribute to a stable global financial and economic environment because of our role as a financial hub.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is, in fact, not just an obligation but it is also in our interest to make a Page: 61 contribution to ensure a stable economic and financial environment which we, in turn, will benefit from.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I should also explain that each member of the IMF is assigned a quota based broadly on its relative size in the world economy, including GDP, openness of its economy and its international reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This quota determines a member's voting power and it is also used as a benchmark for the IMF to apportion potential financial assistance to the IMF.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For instance, the IMF distributed gold sale proceeds to members in proportion to their quotas to be re-contributed to the PRGT, as I have explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is precisely for accountability and transparency that we want to make sure that the publication is made not just in a Gazette but to ensure that members of the public are informed of what we are doing and there can be a robust debate to Parliament, if need be.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is obliged to repay immediately and fully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the event that such a scenario arises, where we have a balance of payments need, that is the obligation of the IMF to repay immediately and fully.
